questions.stem: How do mutation and sexual reproduction contribute differently to variation?

options.text: Mutation creates new alleles, while sexual reproduction produces new combinations of alleles
options.why: Mutation can add a new allele to the gene pool. Meiosis and fertilization reshuffle alleles that already exist.

options.text: Mutation reshuffles existing alleles, while sexual reproduction creates new alleles
options.why: The roles are reversed. Mutation can create alleles, while sexual reproduction rearranges them into new combinations.

options.text: Mutation creates useful traits, while sexual reproduction removes harmful traits
options.why: Mutations aren't produced according to usefulness. Selection, rather than sexual reproduction itself, changes how common alleles become.

options.text: Mutation changes phenotypes, while sexual reproduction leaves genetic variation unchanged
options.why: Sexual reproduction creates genetic variation among offspring through meiosis and fertilization. It doesn't leave allele combinations unchanged.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies what changes during evolution by natural selection?

options.text: Individual organisms change their alleles during life
options.why: Individuals don't replace their alleles to match the environment. Selection acts on differences already present among individuals.

options.text: Populations change in allele frequency across generations
options.why: Individuals with some heritable variants leave more offspring, so the population's allele frequencies change over generations.

options.text: Ecosystems choose which mutations a species will need
options.why: Environments don't direct mutations. They create conditions in which existing variants differ in survival and reproductive success.

options.text: Species acquire identical adaptations within one generation
options.why: Evolution occurs across generations and depends on heritable variation. Members of a species don't all acquire the same adaptation together.

questions.stem: Which individual has the greatest biological fitness?

options.text: The individual that lives longest but produces no offspring
options.why: Longevity alone doesn't pass alleles forward. An individual producing no offspring has no direct reproductive fitness.

options.text: The individual that is largest and defeats the most competitors
options.why: Size and competitive strength matter only if they increase reproductive success. They aren't definitions of fitness.

options.text: The individual that contributes the most surviving offspring to the next generation
options.why: Fitness is reproductive success relative to others. The key measure is genetic contribution to later generations.

options.text: The individual that changes its phenotype most when conditions change
options.why: Phenotypic change during life isn't the definition of fitness. Its effect on reproductive success would have to be known.

questions.stem: Why doesn't a suntan normally contribute to evolution by natural selection?

options.text: A suntan always reduces the individual's chance of survival
options.why: Its usefulness isn't the issue. The problem is whether the acquired change has a genetic basis that offspring inherit.

options.text: A suntan develops only after the individual has reproduced
options.why: A tan can develop before reproduction. Timing doesn't explain why the acquired pigmentation isn't genetically transmitted.

options.text: A suntan is an acquired change rather than an inherited base-sequence change
options.why: Exposure changes pigment production in the individual's skin, but it doesn't encode the tan in the DNA passed through gametes.

options.text: A suntan occurs in one organism rather than an entire species
options.why: A heritable mutation can begin in one organism and still affect evolution. The missing requirement here is inheritance.

questions.stem: How can female preference for elaborate male plumage change a bird population?

options.text: Preferred males reproduce more, increasing alleles associated with the plumage
options.why: Mate choice creates differential reproductive success. If the plumage is heritable, its associated alleles can increase in frequency.

options.text: Preferred males survive longer, preventing mutation in their offspring
options.why: Sexual selection concerns mating success, and it doesn't prevent mutation. Elaborate plumage may even carry a survival cost.

options.text: Females transfer their preference directly into the males' genes
options.why: Mate choice doesn't rewrite a male's genes. It changes which males contribute alleles to the next generation.

options.text: Males develop brighter feathers after observing the female preference
options.why: That describes an acquired response to need. Evolution requires heritable variation in plumage and differential reproduction.

questions.stem: What outcome is expected for conspicuous male guppies under strong predation?

options.text: They gain both greater mating success and greater survival
options.why: Conspicuousness may attract females, but it can also attract predators. The two effects can oppose one another.

options.text: They are detected more easily, favoring less conspicuous males
options.why: Strong predation raises the survival cost of conspicuous coloration, so less visible males may leave more offspring overall.

options.text: They mutate into duller forms after predators detect them
options.why: Individuals don't mutate their coloration in response to detection. Selection changes the frequencies of heritable variants over generations.

options.text: They eliminate sexual selection from every later generation
options.why: Female choice can still operate under predation. The outcome depends on the balance between mating advantage and survival cost.

questions.stem: What is included in a population's gene pool?

options.text: All genes and their different alleles in the population
options.why: The gene pool includes the genetic variants carried across the whole population, not those from one individual.

options.text: Only alleles that improve survival in the current environment
options.why: Disadvantageous and neutral alleles remain part of the gene pool while they are present in the population.

options.text: Only genes carried by individuals that produce offspring
options.why: The gene pool describes the whole population at a given time, including individuals that may not reproduce.

options.text: All acquired characteristics shared by members of the population
options.why: Acquired characteristics aren't genes or alleles. A gene pool refers to genetic information in the population.

questions.stem: Why can geographically isolated populations develop different allele frequencies?

options.text: Isolation forces both populations to acquire the same mutations
options.why: Mutations aren't directed by isolation, and separate populations needn't receive the same mutations.

options.text: Isolation stops every form of selection within either population
options.why: Selection continues within isolated populations. Different environments can expose them to different selection pressures.

options.text: Reduced gene flow lets selection and genetic drift act independently
options.why: With little exchange of alleles, separate mutations, chance events and selection pressures can make the populations diverge.

options.text: Reduced competition makes every allele equally successful in reproduction
options.why: Isolation doesn't remove competition or equalize reproductive success. Selection can remain strong in either population.

questions.stem: A selection pressure favors both extreme phenotypes and acts against intermediate phenotypes. Which pattern is this?

options.text: Directional selection
options.why: Directional selection favors one extreme and shifts the distribution toward that side.

options.text: Stabilizing selection
options.why: Stabilizing selection favors intermediate phenotypes and acts against both extremes.

options.text: Disruptive selection
options.why: Disruptive selection favors both extremes, so the phenotype distribution tends to develop two peaks.

options.text: Artificial selection
options.why: Artificial selection describes deliberate human choice of breeding individuals, not this pattern of phenotypic selection.

questions.stem: In the Hardy–Weinberg equation, what does 2pq represent?

options.text: The frequency of the dominant allele
options.why: One allele frequency is represented by p. Dominance doesn't determine which letter must be used.

options.text: The frequency of the recessive allele
options.why: One allele frequency is represented by q. The term 2pq combines both allele frequencies.

options.text: The frequency of the heterozygous genotype
options.why: A heterozygote can receive either allele from either parent, giving the combined expected frequency 2pq.

options.text: The frequency of both homozygous genotypes
options.why: The homozygous genotype frequencies are p² and q². Their sum isn't represented by 2pq.

questions.stem: In a Hardy–Weinberg population, 16% of individuals have genotype aa. What is the frequency of allele A?

options.why: The value 0.16 is q², the frequency of genotype aa. It isn't an allele frequency.
Taking the square root gives q = 0.40, which is the frequency of allele a.
Because q² = 0.16, q = 0.40. Therefore p, the frequency of A, equals 1 − 0.40 = 0.60.
Subtracting q² directly from 1 mixes genotype and allele frequencies. You must find q before calculating p.

questions.stem: Which set contains only Hardy–Weinberg conditions?

options.text: Large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration and no natural selection
options.why: Together these conditions prevent systematic or chance changes from disturbing the expected allele and genotype frequencies.

options.text: Small population, random mating, frequent mutation, no migration and stabilizing selection
options.why: A small population permits genetic drift, while mutation and selection violate the equilibrium conditions.

options.text: Large population, selective mating, no mutation, frequent migration and no competition
options.why: Selective mating violates random mating, and migration introduces or removes alleles through gene flow.

options.text: Stable population size, sexual reproduction, no predators, no disease and unlimited food
options.why: Those ecological conditions aren't the Hardy–Weinberg assumptions. They omit mutation, migration and random mating.

questions.stem: Why is antibiotic resistance classified as natural selection rather than artificial selection?

options.text: Bacteria deliberately choose resistance when an antibiotic appears
options.why: Bacteria don't choose genetic changes. Resistant variants survive the selection pressure more successfully.

options.text: Humans select individual resistant bacteria and breed them together
options.why: That would resemble artificial selection, but antibiotic treatment doesn't involve choosing bacterial parents.

options.text: Antibiotics create resistance alleles in every exposed bacterium
options.why: Antibiotics don't direct the required mutation. They reduce susceptible bacteria and favor resistant variants.

options.text: Antibiotics favor resistant variants without deliberate choice of breeders
options.why: Humans create the selection pressure, but differential survival and reproduction determine which bacterial alleles spread.

questions.stem: A drought begins, and plants with a heritable water-conserving trait produce more seeds. What is the expected long-term outcome?

options.text: Every plant develops the trait because water has become scarce
options.why: Need doesn't make every individual acquire a heritable trait. Variation must already arise through genetic processes.

options.text: The drought creates the same beneficial mutation in every seed
options.why: Mutation isn't directed toward the population's needs. The drought acts as a selection pressure on variation.

options.text: The water-conserving allele increases in frequency across generations
options.why: Plants carrying the heritable trait leave more offspring, so their associated allele contributes more copies to later generations.

options.text: The population reaches Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium through natural selection
options.why: Natural selection violates a Hardy–Weinberg condition. Selection is expected to change allele frequencies rather than maintain equilibrium.
